Lessons.Title: Different Square Units (Part 1) — Inches Versus Centimeters
ExplanationParagraphs: IM K–5 2021 first-edition Grade 3 Unit 2 Lesson 6, source standard 3.MD.C.6. Original Student Task Statements is 3 pages. Compare area units with physical sides of one inch versus one centimeter. First-party Edulytics material is independently authored.

Warm-up, Notice and Wonder (10 minutes): four actual 2021 source diagrams have been visually inspected, showing the SAME outer rectangular region partitioned into 5×10=50, 3×6=18, 2×4=8, and 1×2=2 SQUARE units. The four square-unit sizes differ, so the numerical tile counts differ even though the covered physical region is identical. The first-party visualization draws the same 2:1 outer rectangle in four mathematically equivalent subdivisions without copying publisher art.

Activity 1: Same Rectangle, Different Units (15 minutes). Original blackline PDF contains square-INCH paper (1-inches sides) and square-CENTIMETER paper (1-cm sides). Partner 1 uses grid 1 and partner 2 grid 2; EACH draws separately 2×5 (10 cells), 7×3 (21 cells), and 6×8 (48 cells). Those counts are equal but the corresponding physical areas differ because square inches are larger than square centimeters. Each pair measures their printed square side lengths with rulers. MLR8 Discussion Supports asks pupils to restate peers' observations precisely using 'area'.

Activity 2: What's the Area? (20 minutes). Original 2021 learner paper requires FIRST estimating how many square inches and square centimeters tile its original approximately two-inch-sided square, THEN tracing or cutting the square and overlaying on each grid, THEN recording two physical measurements and TWO row-by-column expressions — one for each unit. An exactly two-inch by two-inch square is four in², but its theoretical exact cm² area is 25.8064, NOT exactly 25; no publisher original student response is graded to a fixed centimeter integer. Teacher evaluates the actual observations, precision and the multiplication models.

MLR2 Collect and Display gathers phrases about square inch, square centimeter and how a smaller square unit requires MORE tiles of the same region. Action and Expression provides physical 1-inch tiles and 1-centimeter cube faces; source materials include rulers, scissors, tracing/patty paper and a fresh original unit-grid handout. Lesson synthesis asks when and why different area units are useful.

Original teacher reflection asks which question could have improved the lesson; suggested optional centers: Capture Squares Stage 6 (multiply 1–5), Rectangle Rumble Stage 1 (factors 1,2,5,10), and Five in a Row Addition and Subtraction Stage 6. Publisher's educator-gated Which Square? Cool-down is not duplicated. The Edulytics 21 cm² and 24 in² checks are independent first-party skill equivalents, and their human-drawn diagrams still require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Square inch
KeyConcepts.Definition: A 2D unit region, exactly one inch on each side.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use 'in²'; both sides count square inches, not inches.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 2×2 grid of inch squares has area 4 in².

KeyConcepts.Title: Square centimeter
KeyConcepts.Definition: A 2D unit region, exactly one centimeter on each side.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use 'cm²'; square centimeters are physically smaller than square inches.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same numerical count, different physical area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Counts of equal-sized squares require naming the square-unit size.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Twenty-one square inches occupy more plane space than twenty-one square centimeters.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two pupils draw 7×3 on different-size 2021 physical grid papers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same area can have different unit counts
KeyConcepts.Definition: The physical region stays the same while unit size changes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Smaller tiles require more squares for the same region.

KeyConcepts.Title: Measurement is a physical process
KeyConcepts.Definition: Estimation, tracing, grid-overlay and explanation are independently assessed steps.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not replace the original empirical centimeter measurement with an automatically graded 25.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two-inch square =4 in², theoretical 25.8064 cm², actual print/overlay teacher checked.

WorkedExamples.Title: One region, four tilings
WorkedExamples.Question: How can the 2021 A,B,C,D figures have 50,18,8,2 cells but identical boundaries?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use equal outer dimensions and different-size unit squares.
Steps: All four cover the same original outer rectangle.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Same region, different square-unit sizes and counts.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher examines source figure and justifications.

WorkedExamples.Title: Both grids for three expressions
WorkedExamples.Question: Create 2×5,7×3,6×8 on original inch and centimeter paper.
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw separately on both grids and physically compare.
Steps: 2×5=10 square units on EACH physical grid.
Say 10/21/48 in² for inch paper and 10/21/48 cm² for centimeter paper.
Identical counts are not identical physical areas.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 10,21,48 in² and cm² respectively, from different paper sizes.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original square measured two ways
WorkedExamples.Question: Estimate and measure source square with inch and centimeter grids.
WorkedExamples.Method: Estimate separately, cut/trace, overlay, then describe rows and columns.
Steps: With exact two-inch sides, area is 2×2=4 in².
For the same physical region, the square centimeter count is larger; theoretical exact 25.8064 cm².
Record empirical centimeter measurement without false exact integer claim.
Write two multiplication expressions and label correct square units.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 4 in² for exact two-inch square, and approximate/observed cm² subject to human review.
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not auto-grade original source centimeter measurement to 25.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating counts 50,18,8,2 as different physical areas.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original source A–D have the same outer rectangle, but different square-unit sizes.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare the enclosed region, then name the size of each square unit.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The unit squares are physically different in size.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare measured square side lengths; name unit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming original drawn square's centimeter area exactly equals 25.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Theoretical 2-inch square is 25.8064 cm², and paper measurements vary.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Do not invent a strict centimeter count; teacher checks overlay measurements.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Submitting only '21' for a prompt asking for 21 cm².
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An area measurement must include the correct unit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Skipping estimates and two observed physical-grid measurements.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source demands an actual measurement investigation and two multiplication expressions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Collect estimates, measure on both original unit grids, compare and explain.

SummaryPoints: 2021 first-edition Student Task Statements 3 pages, original four warm-up grids, and original dual-size unit-grid blackline master inspected.
Same rectangle illustrated with 50,18,8,2 differently-sized square regions.
Pairs draw 2×5,7×3 and 6×8 on BOTH inch and centimeter grids.
An exact 2-in by 2-in square is 4 in² but not exactly 25 cm²; original centimeter measurements are teacher-reviewed, not auto-scored.
MLR2 Collect and Display, MLR8 language restatements and teacher-reviewed physical measurement retained.
First-party independent Practice/Cool-down use strict written square units: 21 cm² and 24 in².
Source artwork and educator-gated Cool-down are not copied; no .NET tests/CI, Stage D, deployment or academic sign-off.
